nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; poet and professor, teaching in Leeds and then at Boston University from 1988, writing in English
literary_identity: English poet of history, guilt and the religious conscience, whose dense, formally exact poems from For the Unfallen to Broken Hierarchies made him the most admired and most difficult poet of his generation
biography: Geoffrey William Hill was born on 18 June 1932 in Bromsgrove, Worcestershire, the son of a policeman, and grew up in the Worcestershire village of Fairfield. He read English at Keble College, Oxford, where he was taught by F. W. Bateson, and worked as a schoolteacher and lecturer before becoming a professor of English at Leeds, where he taught from 1981 to 1988. His first collection, For the Unfallen, appeared in 1959 from the Fantasy Press, and established the historical and elegiac manner of his early work; King Log (1968), which won the Hawthornden Prize, was followed by Mercian Hymns (1971), a sequence of thirty prose poems about Offa, king of Mercia, and his own childhood, Tenebrae (1978), The Mystery of the Charity of Charles Péguy (1983), the Collected Poems (1985), Canaan (1996), The Triumph of Love (1998), Speech! Speech! (2000), The Orchards of Syracuse (2002), A Treatise of Civil Power (2007), Odi Barbare (2012) and The Book of Baruch by the Gnostic Justin (2015); his poems were gathered in Broken Hierarchies: Poems 1952-2012 (2013). He taught at Boston University from 1988 and died in Cambridge on 30 June 2016.
literary_profile: Poetry: For the Unfallen (1959), Preghiere (1964), King Log (1968), Mercian Hymns (1971), Tenebrae (1978), The Mystery of the Charity of Charles Péguy (1983), Collected Poems (1985), Canaan (1996), The Triumph of Love (1998), Speech! Speech! (2000), The Orchards of Syracuse (2002), A Treatise of Civil Power (2007), Odi Barbare (2012) and The Book of Baruch by the Gnostic Justin (2015); Broken Hierarchies: Poems 1952-2012 (2013). Criticism: The Lords of Limit (1984), The Enemy's Country (1991) and Style and Faith (2003).
stylistic_characteristics: Dense, allusive, syntactically compressed verse in strict forms; the early poems in regular stanzas and pentameters, the later in a baroque, punning, self-interrogating free verse; a vocabulary drawn from law, theology, music and etymology; the prose poems of Mercian Hymns; a habit of quotation and of echoing earlier English poets.
intellectual_concerns: History as guilt and complicity, from the Wars of the Roses to the Holocaust and the twentieth-century state; the English past and the English landscape (Offa's Mercia, the Welsh border); religious faith, grace and theology, especially in Tenebrae; the poet's vocation and its compromised relation to power and money; language itself as a fallen, contested inheritance.
historical_significance: The most highly regarded English poet of his generation, the central figure in the revival of a difficult, historically conscious and religiously serious poetry after the Movement, and a poet whose later work divided readers into those who found in it the fullest statement of the century's guilt and those who found it obscure, bombastic and increasingly a poetry of commentary rather than creation.
bibliographical_notes: The books are listed from Wikipedia's bibliography and checked against the contents of Broken Hierarchies (2013) for the poems of 1959 and 1968. Installment 10 records only the three dated Norton selections ('In Memory of Jane Fraser' and 'Requiem for the Plantagenet Kings', 1959; 'September Song', 1968), so the bibliography is incomplete; 'Broken Hierarchies' (the 2013 collection) is undated in the Norton list and is not recorded. The prose and the later collections have no records.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Australian; poet, anthologist and critic writing in English
literary_identity: Australian poet of the bush, the suburb, the Aboriginal world and the English language itself, whose nearly thirty volumes made him the leading Australian poet of his generation
biography: Leslie Allan Murray was born on 17 October 1938 at Nabiac, on the north coast of New South Wales, and grew up on his family's dairy farm at Bunyah, in the Manning River valley, a landscape that remained the ground of his poetry. His mother died when he was twelve, an event that recurs in his work. He was educated at Taree High School and the University of Sydney, where he read German and English, and travelled to Europe in the late 1950s. His first collection, The Ilex Tree (1965), was written with Geoffrey Lehmann; The Weatherboard Cathedral (1969), Lunch and Counter Lunch (1974), The Vernacular Republic (1976), Ethnic Radio (1977), The People's Otherworld (1983), The Daylight Moon (1987), Dog Fox Field (1990), Translations from the Natural World (1992), Subhuman Redneck Poems (1996, T. S. Eliot Prize), Conscious and Verbal (1999), Poems the Size of Photographs (2002), Fredy Neptune (1998, a verse novel), The Biplane Houses (2006), Taller When Prone (2010) and Waiting for the Past (2015) followed. He was a noted anthologist, editor of the journal Quadrant and a controversial essayist, and lived at Bunyah, where he returned in 1985, and later at Taree. He died on 29 April 2019.
literary_profile: Poetry: The Ilex Tree (1965, with Geoffrey Lehmann), The Weatherboard Cathedral (1969), Poems Against Economics (1972), Lunch and Counter Lunch (1974), The Vernacular Republic (1976), Ethnic Radio (1977), The Boys Who Stole the Funeral (1980), The People's Otherworld (1983), The Daylight Moon (1987), Dog Fox Field (1990), Translations from the Natural World (1992), Subhuman Redneck Poems (1996), Conscious and Verbal (1999), Poems the Size of Photographs (2002), The Biplane Houses (2006), Taller When Prone (2010) and Waiting for the Past (2015); the verse novels The Boys Who Stole the Funeral (1980) and Fredy Neptune (1998), and the Collected Poems (2018). Prose: The Peasant Mandarin (1978), Persistence in Folly (1984) and A Working Forest (1997).
stylistic_characteristics: Long, rhythmically insistent free verse and loose stanza forms, with a strongly percussive, alliterative music and a taste for strange compounds and lists; a diction that moves between the demotic Australian and the ornate; narrative and satirical poems as well as lyrics; the 'translations from the natural world' in the voices of animals.
intellectual_concerns: The Australian landscape and the rural life of the Manning valley; the vernacular and the survival of Aboriginal culture; class, the suburbs and the 'barbecue of the ordinary'; religion, Catholicism and the sacramental; depression, illness and the body; the English language as a living, plural inheritance.
historical_significance: The leading Australian poet of his generation and the only one to have won the T. S. Eliot Prize, Murray's work was central to the emergence of a distinctively Australian poetry in the 1970s and 1980s; his vernacular nationalism and his political essays made him a controversial public figure, but his best poems are among the most original in postwar English poetry.
bibliographical_notes: The collections are listed from Wikipedia, the contents of Collected Poems (2018) and general knowledge. Installment 10 records only the two Norton selections, 'Morse' (The People's Otherworld, 1983) and 'Corniche' (Subhuman Redneck Poems, 1996); 'The Kitchen Grammars' (2006) is outside the period. The bibliography is therefore incomplete, and the verse novels and prose have no records.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; novelist, short-story writer and essayist writing in English, resident at Shepperton from 1960
literary_identity: English novelist of the 'inner space' and the disaster, who took science fiction into the terrain of psychology, consumer culture and the media, from The Drowned World to Crash and Empire of the Sun
biography: James Graham Ballard was born on 15 November 1930 in the Shanghai International Settlement, where his father managed a chemical company, and spent the war years in the Lunghua internment camp after the Japanese occupation of the city, an experience he later used in Empire of the Sun (1984). He was sent to England in 1946, educated at The Leys School in Cambridge and read medicine at King's College, Cambridge, intending to become a psychiatrist, before leaving for London and working as an advertising copywriter and on a trade journal. His first stories appeared in New Worlds in the late 1950s, and The Wind from Nowhere (1961) and The Drowned World (1962) made his name as a writer of catastrophe fiction; The Drought (1965) and The Crystal World (1966) completed the sequence. The Atrocity Exhibition (1970), Crash (1973), Concrete Island (1974) and High-Rise (1975) turned to the 'inner space' of the media landscape and the eroticism of technology, while Empire of the Sun (1984) and The Kindness of Women (1991) returned to Shanghai. His later novels include Cocaine Nights (1996), Super-Cannes (2000) and Millennium People (2003). He died at Shepperton on 19 April 2009.
literary_profile: Novels: The Wind from Nowhere (1961), The Drowned World (1962), The Drought (1965), The Crystal World (1966), The Atrocity Exhibition (1970), Crash (1973), Concrete Island (1974), High-Rise (1975), The Unlimited Dream Company (1979), Hello America (1981), Empire of the Sun (1984), The Day of Creation (1987), Running Wild (1988), The Kindness of Women (1991), Rushing to Paradise (1994), Cocaine Nights (1996), Super-Cannes (2000), Millennium People (2003) and Kingdom Come (2006). Stories: The Voices of Time (1962), Billenium (1962), The Four-Dimensional Nightmare (1963), The Terminal Beach (1964), The Disaster Area (1967), The Overloaded Man (1967), Vermilion Sands (1971) and The Complete Short Stories (2001). Nonfiction: A User's Guide to the Millennium (1996) and Miracles of Life (2008).
stylistic_characteristics: A cool, exact, medically precise prose, with a clinician's detachment from violence and sex; the imagery of drained pools, empty motorways, abandoned airports and flooded cities; the rejection of character psychology in favour of 'inner space'; the short story built as a sequence of tableaux; the late novels in a plainer, more conventional narrative mode.
intellectual_concerns: Catastrophe as revelation: the flood, the drought, the crystallising forest and the emptied city reveal what the society concealed; the psychology of the media, of celebrity and of violence (The Atrocity Exhibition, Crash); the erosion of the boundary between the human and the technological; childhood, imprisonment and survival (Empire of the Sun); the gated community and the pathology of affluence in the late novels.
historical_significance: The most important British science-fiction writer of the postwar period and the one who did most to move the genre into the mainstream of literary fiction; the adjective 'Ballardian' has entered the dictionaries, and his catastrophe novels of the 1960s are now read as founding texts of climate fiction.
bibliographical_notes: The books are listed from Wikipedia and general knowledge, with the publication details of The Drowned World checked against its own article. Installment 10 records only the Norton selection, The Drowned World (1962), so the bibliography is incomplete; the stories, the later novels and the essays have no records, and the dates of first publication were not checked title by title.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: South African-born; short-story writer and novelist who lived in Botswana from 1964 and became a Botswana citizen in 1979, writing in English
literary_identity: South African-born writer of Botswana whose novels and stories of Serowe, from When Rain Clouds Gather to A Question of Power, made her one of the most original voices of southern African fiction
biography: Bessie Amelia Emery Head was born on 6 July 1937 in Pietermaritzburg, Natal, the daughter of a white woman and a black man, and was raised in foster homes and then in a mission orphanage after her mother was committed to a mental hospital. She trained as a teacher at a mission college in Durban and taught in Natal and in the Cape, and worked as a journalist in Cape Town and Johannesburg, where she was associated with the Pan Africanist Congress and wrote for its paper. She left South Africa in 1964 on a one-way exit permit, taught in Serowe, in Bechuanaland (now Botswana), and settled there, writing in poverty and isolation. Her first novel, When Rain Clouds Gather, appeared in 1968, followed by Maru (1971) and A Question of Power (1973), the last a harrowing account of mental breakdown that made her reputation; The Collector of Treasures and Other Botswana Village Tales (1977) and Serowe: Village of the Rain Wind (1981) drew on the history and oral tradition of her adopted home, and her posthumous works include Tales of Tenderness and Power (1989), A Woman Alone (1990) and The Cardinals (1993). She became a Botswana citizen in 1979 and died in Serowe on 17 April 1986.
literary_profile: Novels: When Rain Clouds Gather (1968), Maru (1971) and A Question of Power (1973). Stories: The Collector of Treasures and Other Botswana Village Tales (1977) and Tales of Tenderness and Power (1989, posthumous). Nonfiction and oral history: Serowe: Village of the Rain Wind (1981). Letters and journalism: A Woman Alone (1990) and A Gesture of Belonging (1991).
stylistic_characteristics: A spare, translucent prose that moves without strain between realistic village narrative and visionary or hallucinated interior states; the short story built as a parable or a folk tale told by a narrator close to the community; direct speech in a Botswana idiom; a moral clarity that is never merely schematic.
intellectual_concerns: Racial and sexual oppression in southern Africa; the position of women in village society and their resistance (The Collector of Treasures); madness, spiritual crisis and the divided self (A Question of Power); drought, poverty and survival; exile, belonging and the possibility of a just community.
historical_significance: One of the central writers of southern African fiction in English and, with Bessie Head's own account of mental illness, one of the first African novelists to write from inside a breakdown; her stories are widely anthologised and taught, and she is regarded as Botswana's most influential writer.
bibliographical_notes: The books are listed from Wikipedia and general knowledge; only the Norton selection, 'Looking for a Rain God' (in The Collector of Treasures, 1977), has a work record, so the bibliography is incomplete. The posthumous volumes were not checked title by title, and no text of the story was consulted beyond the synopsis cited in its record.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Nigerian-born British; novelist, short-story writer, poet and essayist writing in English, resident in London from 1978
literary_identity: Nigerian-born novelist of the spirit world and the Nigerian street, whose The Famished Road won the Booker Prize in 1991 and whose stories of the 1980s made him the leading inheritor of Tutuola's fabulous mode
biography: Ben Golden Emuobowho Okri was born on 15 March 1959 in Minna, in what is now Niger State, Nigeria, and grew up in Lagos and Ibadan, where his father, a clerk, moved the family; he has described a childhood of crowded compound life, of stories told by his mother and of the Nigerian civil war, which he witnessed as a child. He moved to England in 1978 and read comparative literature at the University of Essex, and published his first novel, Flowers and Shadows, in 1980, followed by The Landscapes Within (1981). The short-story collection Incidents at the Shrine (1986) and Stars of the New Curfew (1988) established his voice, and The Famished Road (1991), the first of a trilogy with Songs of Enchantment (1993) and Infinite Riches (1998), won the Booker Prize. Later work includes Astonishing the Gods (1995), Dangerous Love (1996), A Way of Being Free (1997), Starbook (2007), The Age of Magic (2008) and The Freedom Artist (2019), with poetry in An African Elegy (1992), Mental Fight (1999) and A Fire in My Head (2021). He was awarded the OBE in 2001 and knighted in 2023.
literary_profile: Novels: Flowers and Shadows (1980), The Landscapes Within (1981), The Famished Road (1991), Songs of Enchantment (1993), Astonishing the Gods (1995), Infinite Riches (1998), Starbook (2007), The Age of Magic (2008) and The Freedom Artist (2019). Stories: Incidents at the Shrine (1986), Stars of the New Curfew (1988) and Prayer for the Living (2019). Poetry: An African Elegy (1992), Mental Fight (1999) and A Fire in My Head (2021). Essays: A Way of Being Free (1997) and A Time for New Dreams (2011).
stylistic_characteristics: A dense, lyrical, incantatory prose that draws on Yoruba myth, the ghost story and the oral tale; a first-person narration poised between dream and street; catalogue, repetition and proverb; a refusal of the conventions of the realist novel in favour of the fabulous and the parabolic.
intellectual_concerns: The spirit world and its intrusion into the world of the living (The Famished Road); poverty, corruption and the exploitation of the poor in the Nigerian oil economy ('What the Tapster Saw'); childhood, hunger and survival; myth, prophecy and the artist's vocation; freedom, dreams and the possibility of transformation.
historical_significance: The best-known African novelist of his generation in Britain, and the writer who carried Amos Tutuola's fabulous mode into the postmodern novel; the Booker Prize of 1991 made him an international figure, and his short stories of the 1980s are now read as early examples of what critics call 'petro-magic realism'.
bibliographical_notes: The books are listed from Wikipedia and general knowledge; only the Norton selection, 'What the Tapster Saw' (in Stars of the New Curfew, 1988), has a work record, so the bibliography is incomplete. The story collections' dates were checked against the cited study material, but the novels were not checked title by title.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Indian; novelist and political essayist writing in English
literary_identity: Indian novelist and activist whose first novel, The God of Small Things (1997), won the Booker Prize and gave Indian writing in English one of its most widely read and formally distinctive books
biography: Suzanna Arundhati Roy was born on 24 November 1961 in Shillong, in Assam, the daughter of Mary Roy, a Syrian Christian teacher and women's rights campaigner from Kerala, and a Bengali Hindu tea planter; her parents separated when she was two, and she grew up with her mother and brother in Ayemenem, in Kerala, where the family ran a small factory and a pickle business, and where her mother founded a school. She trained as an architect at the School of Planning and Architecture in New Delhi, worked as a designer, and wrote the screenplays for the films In Which Annie Gives It Those Ones (1989) and Electric Moon (1992), and acted in Masay Sahib (1992). The God of Small Things, published in 1997, won the Booker Prize and became the best-selling book by a non-expatriate Indian author. Since then she has written chiefly political essays and books, including The End of Imagination (1998), The Algebra of Infinite Justice (2001), Power Politics (2001), War Talk (2003), An Ordinary Person's Guide to Empire (2004), Field Notes on Democracy (2009), Broken Republic (2011), Capitalism: A Ghost Story (2014), The Doctor and the Saint (2017) and Azadi (2020), and the novel The Ministry of Utmost Happiness (2017). She won the Sydney Peace Prize in 2004 and the PEN Pinter Prize in 2024, and is a leading campaigner on the Narmada dams, Kashmir and civil liberties.
literary_profile: Fiction: The God of Small Things (1997) and The Ministry of Utmost Happiness (2017). Nonfiction: The End of Imagination (1998), The Cost of Living (1999), The Algebra of Infinite Justice (2001), Power Politics (2001), War Talk (2003), An Ordinary Person's Guide to Empire (2004), Public Power in the Age of Empire (2004), Field Notes on Democracy (2009), Broken Republic (2011), Walking with the Comrades (2011), Capitalism: A Ghost Story (2014), The Doctor and the Saint (2017) and Azadi (2020). Screenplays: In Which Annie Gives It Those Ones (1989) and Electric Moon (1992).
stylistic_characteristics: A prose of great syntactic agility, moving between the child's-eye view and the retrospective narrator's irony; word-play, puns and typographic games (capital letters used as emphasis in the manner of children's speech); a non-linear chronology that withholds its catastrophe; the essay written in a direct, polemical, often sarcastic first person.
intellectual_concerns: The caste and class order of Kerala and the 'love laws' that punish transgression (The God of Small Things); childhood, twins and a divided family; the position of women and of the 'untouchable' in Indian society; colonial and post-colonial power, and the history of the Syrian Christian community; in the essays, globalisation, dams, nuclear weapons and the Indian state's violence.
historical_significance: The God of Small Things was the most celebrated Indian novel in English of its decade, the first by an Indian woman to win the Booker Prize, and a book that changed the market for Indian writing in English. Roy has since become one of the most prominent writer-activists in the world, and her essays are central to the literature of globalisation and dissent.

Installment 10 records only the Norton selection, The God of Small Things (1997), for the extract the anthology prints under the title God's Own Country; the bibliography is therefore incomplete, and the essay collections have no records. The dates of the essays were not checked one by one.
